analysis.one_liner: Caps monthly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $250 per person.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on November 9, 2023 and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit how much patients can be made to pay out of pocket for prescription drugs: no more than $250 per person per month, or $500 per family, in plans sold on the Affordable Care Act marketplaces and in employer-sponsored health plans. The cap would rise each year with medical inflation. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: People who take expensive prescription drugs and are covered by employer health plans or Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. Today, a patient on a costly specialty drug can face cost-sharing of well over $250 a month; this bill would put a hard ceiling on that monthly bill and raise it only with medical inflation. Family members would be protected by a $500 monthly family cap.

how_it_helps.text: Caps prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month ($500 per family) for plan years beginning in 2025, in Affordable Care Act marketplace plans.
Extends the same monthly cap to employer group health plans by tying their cost-sharing limits to the new ACA rules.
Adjusts the cap each year after 2025 by the medical care component of the consumer price index, so the protection does not quietly erode with inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group plans would absorb the difference between what they can now charge patients in deductibles and copays and the new $250 monthly ceiling. Insurers would likely pass part of that cost back to everyone through higher premiums, and employers might shift more into premiums or wages. The bill does nothing to lower the underlying prices drug makers charge, so the money still flows to drug companies — it just comes from a different pocket.

drawbacks.text: The cap limits what patients pay but not what drugs cost: insurers and employers would bear the difference, and much of it would likely resurface as higher premiums for everyone, including people who take no prescriptions.

A $250 monthly cap still allows up to $3,000 a year per person in drug cost-sharing, a large burden for many households; and because the bill never specified a funding mechanism or premium stabilization, insurers might have responded by narrowing which drugs they cover to steer patients away from expensive ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly patients on high-cost specialty drugs, a hard monthly ceiling would be immediate, tangible relief, and the inflation index would keep it meaningful. The honest cost is that the bill moves money rather than reduces it: drug prices stay untouched, so the expense shifts to insurers, employers, and premium payers, with a real risk that plans respond by restricting access to the priciest drugs. It was a two-page bill with no mechanism to cushion the premium impact, which is a fair criticism even from supporters of the goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Manning introduced the Capping Prescription Costs Act on November 9, 2023; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over health insurance rules.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the last recorded action on the bill.
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it died without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who sponsor health plans are better off because the monthly cost-sharing cap never became law and they avoided absorbing the difference between patient copays and the $250 ceiling. Patients on expensive drugs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers who fund plans

for.name: Rep. Kathy E. Manning
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 9, 2023 to cap monthly prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce (Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters were both Democrats and it never reached a floor vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill caps what insurers can collect from patients in drug copays and deductibles at $250 a month, directly cutting into the cost-sharing they pass on to sick members. Their likely response — raising premiums or narrowing drug coverage — would land on the same people the bill tries to help.

industries.industry: Employers that sponsor group health plans
industries.note: The bill extends the cap to employer plans, so employers would share the added cost with insurers. Employees with expensive prescriptions would see their monthly drug bills capped; premium contributions would likely rise for everyone.
